title: Gather Victim Network Information: DNS
summary: This sub-technique covers the Domain Name System records that describe a victim's naming and mail estate. Mail exchanger, text, and sender policy records routinely disclose which third-party cloud and software services an organisation has adopted, because those services require the organisation to publish verification and routing entries. Adversaries read them through ordinary recursive lookups, through passive DNS datasets that retain historical resolutions long after a record is deleted, and occasionally through a zone transfer, which is a single request that copies every record from a server if that server is misconfigured to allow it. Recursive lookups blend into normal traffic and are essentially indivisible from legitimate resolution, but zone transfer attempts against an authoritative server from an unfamiliar source are a much stronger signal and should be rare. Defenders get the most value from authoritative server logs, where query type mix and source diversity stand out against steady resolver traffic.

beginner.definition: This sub-technique is about reading the Domain Name System (DNS) records of a target. DNS is the service that turns names into addresses. Those records show which name servers, mail servers, and other hosts exist, and which outside services the organisation uses.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most DNS records must be public for the internet to work, so you cannot hide them all. Mail records often name the email provider, which tells an attacker where to aim a phishing campaign. A badly configured server may also hand over its entire record list in one request. That exposes hosts you never meant to advertise.
howItWorks: The attacker queries your name servers for common record types, such as mail and text records.
Mail records point to your email provider, which is often an outside cloud service.
Text records can confirm which cloud or software services your organisation has verified.
They collect passive records from third parties that stored old lookups of your domain.
They try a zone transfer, which asks a server to copy every record at once.
If the server allows it, they receive a full list of your hosts and subdomains.
beginner.example: Picture a village telephone directory. Anyone can read the main switchboard number and the number for the post office. Those entries must be public so that callers can reach them. Now imagine a careless clerk who also keeps the full internal extension list behind the desk. A visitor who asks politely receives a copy of every extension in one go. DNS is the directory for the internet. Mail records are the switchboard number, and they have to be public. A zone transfer is that internal extension list, and it should never be handed to a stranger. Only the requests appear in your server logs.
takeaways: DNS records are public by design, so decide deliberately what each record reveals about your suppliers.
Block zone transfers to unknown hosts and review name server logs for transfer requests.
Passive DNS data keeps old records alive, so deleting a record does not erase its history.

objectives: Explain how DNS record types such as mail exchanger and text records reveal third-party service use.
Describe what a zone transfer is and why a misconfigured name server makes it possible.
Identify the log sources that record DNS reconnaissance and explain their limits.
Distinguish routine recursive resolution from deliberate record enumeration.
Recommend configuration changes that limit what DNS exposes about an organisation.
